# Voice profile — doctorow-blog

**Confidence: full — 10 usable samples, 17,549 corpus words. Voice card: empty; everything below is derived from the corpus.**

---

## 1. Cadence

The sentence that delivers the verdict is short. It arrives after longer sentences have built the mechanism it names — 10/10 samples, several times per piece (`drop-a-dime`: *"Data brokers are a cancer."* — four words, the opening line). When you have run two or three sentences describing how something works, make the sentence that names what it is the shortest one in the paragraph.

The most common hinge for this move is a colon: a long clause states the phenomenon; a colon; a short flat clause names it — 10/10 samples, several times per piece (`posthuman-as-in-no-humans`: *"There's only one kind of person you get to treat like this: a slave."*). The clause before the colon can be a single sentence or an entire paragraph. What the colon commits to is that what follows is short, direct, and not hedged. Build the case; deliver the verdict after the colon.

After a verdict, the next sentence can compress it further — to a definition or a restatement short enough to work as a caption. In `posthuman-as-in-no-humans`, the colon sentence is followed immediately by: *"Slavery is labor without even the pretense of moral consideration."* One sentence names the category; the next defines it in eleven words. Do this when the verdict has a second edge that belongs on its own line.

Anaphoric repetition — beginning consecutive sentences with the same phrase — appears 7/10 samples, once or twice per piece, in a climactic paragraph (`wilhoitian`: *"Politics aren't a bunch of cultural signifiers or identity markers. Politics aren't about who rules – it's about whether we are ruled at all, or whether we are free."*). Use it when the closing argument has two clauses that belong together as a pair.

## 2. How a piece opens

Three opening forms distribute across all 10 samples:

**Blunt declaration** (3/10): The thesis arrives in the first sentence, stated as fact — *"Data brokers are a cancer"* (`drop-a-dime`); *"As a technology, AI isn't exceptional"* (`supplemental-income`); *"'The designated survivor' is one of the weirder aspects of America's (very, very weird) political system"* (`designated-survivor`). The argument begins from the assertion, not toward it.

**"Here's" frame** (2/10): The piece announces what it is about to show — *"Here's an irony: the 'gig economy' is a statistical black hole"* (`your-risk`); *"Here's a sentence that stopped me in my tracks last week:"* (`table-flipper`). A colon delivers the subject without delay.

**Introduction of the term or target** (5/10): The thing to be argued about is named and briefly described before the argument begins — *"One of 2026's better tech-related coinages is 'dickover,' John Gruber's term for…"* (`dickovers`); *"The theory of markets goes like this: even the best of us can fall prey to selfishness and rationalization"* (`lucky-orifices`); *"While the AI bubble is primarily a material phenomenon…"* (`posthuman-as-in-no-humans`). The reader is handed the object before the writer picks it apart.

In all three forms, the subject is on the table in the first two sentences. Do not open by explaining what the piece will argue; open on the thing itself.

## 3. How a piece closes

Eight of ten pieces end by returning to a word or phrase from the opening, now carrying a different or deepened meaning — 8/10 samples. `your-risk` opens on Uber's claim about "flexibility" and closes: *"they value their flexibility, which arises out of the constraints (technical, legal) they impose on us: the drivers and passengers."* `dickovers` closes: *"What they call 'theft' is just self-defense."* The opponent's language is borrowed at the open and returned reversed at the close.

The final sentence is usually short and does not summarize — it delivers. If the argument has done its work, the close needs only to name what just happened.

## 4. Who is being addressed, and how

The reader is *you*, addressed directly throughout every piece — [measurement:second-person-family] 385 instances, 21.94 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, throughout. This is not decorative: it is *your boss*, *your paycheck*, *your own phone*, *your doctor*. The reader is placed inside the situation being described. Write as though speaking to one person who is implicated in the problem.

Alongside the direct *you*, a first-person plural runs that includes the reader on the same side — [measurement:first-person-plural-family] 127 instances, 7.24 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, several times per piece. *"We got rid of pop-ups by installing pop-up blockers"* (`dickovers`); *"we, as a society, have decided this is bad"* (`drop-a-dime`). The *we* signals solidarity: the writer is arguing from inside the same predicament, not lecturing from above. When the piece calls for action, put the writer inside the *we* doing it.

The first person singular — [measurement:first-person-singular-family] 113 instances, 6.44 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, several times per piece — most often marks the writer as an arguer with a position, not a character with a history. When biographical details appear (3/10 samples), they are evidence, not scene-setting: `designated-survivor` discusses cancer, age, and a dead friend because those are the actuarial argument made personal (*"I'm 55. 20 years ago, it was unusual for just one of my peers to die in a given year; now I lose a couple every year."*). In the other 7/10 samples, the writer appears only as arguer. Do not insert biography unless it is the evidence.

Qualification, when it occurs, is first-person rather than adverbial — 10/10 samples. There is no *arguably*, *perhaps*, or *one might say*. Uncertainty is placed on the writer: *"I think billionaire solipsism can account for much of the malinvestment in this obvious bubble, but I don't think it's the whole story"* (`supplemental-income`). When you are not certain, say *"I think"* and keep moving. Do not soften the claim itself with an adverb.

Contractions are near-total — [measurement:contractions] 300 instances, 17.09 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, throughout. Against them, only [measurement:uncontracted-negatives] 9 uncontracted negative phrases across the entire corpus (*do not*, *is not*, *cannot*, *should not*, and similar forms), 0.51 per 1,000 words, present across 10/10 samples as an aggregate rate; they appear in only 5 of the 10 individual samples. The ratio is roughly 33:1 in favor of contractions. Write contracted throughout. Reserve the full uncontracted form for at most one occasion per long piece, where the formality earns something.

Questions are real pressure — [measurement:question-marks] 38 instances, 2.17 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, several times per piece. They are almost never left for the reader to answer; they are answered immediately by the writer, or left as rhetorical pressure on the opponent's premise: *"Why would they operate a hospital if they could go meta and sell the doctorbots to the MBAs running the hospital?"* (`go-meta-meta`). Use a question to put the burden of proof on the premise you are about to dismantle, then answer it yourself in the following sentence.

Profanity is genuine, not decorative — [measurement:profanity-vulgarity] 26 instances, 1.48 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples. It appears in two modes: as the shortest possible verdict (*"This is bullshit"* — multiple samples), and as sudden escalation at the point of maximum absurdity (*"the whole fucking point of this exercise"* — `drop-a-dime`). It is not scattered through exposition. Place it where the situation is most outrageous, and nowhere else.

Opponents are named — proper nouns, not abstractions — 9/10 samples: Uber, Lyft, Musk, Thiel, Trump, Zuckerberg, Tony West. Their words are quoted and then turned against them: *"Tony West isn't lying when he says Uber values flexibility – they value their flexibility"* (`your-risk`). Quote the opponent's language; use their words to make the case against them.

Named allies and sources appear in 9/10 samples: David Weil, John Quiggin, Corey Robin, Steven Brust, Lina Khan, Henry Farrell. Their contributions are attributed with *"as X writes"* or *"X's term for"* — the argument is built in explicit dialogue, not in a vacuum.

## 5. Figures

Images are drawn from four domains, mixed freely within a paragraph — 10/10 samples:

**Medical and biological**: data brokers are *"a cancer"*; centrism is a *"pathology"*; corporate personhood conjures *"immortal, pluripotent colony organisms"*; the AI company *"incubated a foetal demiurge"*. These figures carry a note of diagnostic precision — the thing is being classified, not merely described.

**Economic and legal**: technical terms are introduced in order to be dismantled — *"algorithmic wage discrimination," "revealed preferences," "moats and walls," "consumer welfare"*. The term is quoted; refuting what it conceals is the argument.

**SF and literary**: *"AI Omelas"* (Le Guin); *"immanentizing the eschaton"*; *"Renfields"* (Dracula); *"foal a locomotive"*. These are shorthand for a readership assumed to recognize them. Use them when the comparison is exact and earns its compression; do not explain them.

**Freshly coined or repurposed**: *"dickover," "enshittify," "disenshittify," "the word-guessing program"* (for AI), *"god-botherers," "emerged from a lucky orifice."* Coinages name what the opponent would not call by its right name. Coin when an existing term would protect the thing you are describing.

A figure runs one clause and is not reopened — 10/10 samples. The extended escrow-agent analogy in `table-flipper` runs several paragraphs, but it is the structuring device of that section, not a passing image; it is the exception, not a license to extend figures generally.

## 6. Register range

The prose moves between analytical and polemical within the same paragraph — 10/10 samples. The analytical mode explains how a mechanism works; the polemical mode names what it is doing to people. Neither stands alone: the analysis charges the accusation, the accusation justifies the analysis.

Technical register is not translated into vagueness — 8/10 samples. GDPR, SWIFT, CFPB, DMCA, algorithmic wage discrimination, Convention 193 — the law, the court, the decision, the company name — are named. Knowing the mechanism in precise detail is what makes the charge land. Do not round down to a vague noun where the specific term exists.

Parenthetical spans carry irony, asides, and sudden escalations without breaking the sentence — [measurement:round-parenthetical-spans] 97 instances, 5.53 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, throughout: *(very, very weird)*; *(a direct quote)*; *(gasp!)*. A parenthetical belongs where the aside is too sharp to drop but too small to promote into its own sentence. At 5.53 per 1,000 words, that is roughly one every 180 words — use them at that rate, not more.

Interruption and elaboration within sentences is carried by en-dashes, not em-dashes — [measurement:en-dashes] 73 instances, 4.16 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, several times per piece. Em-dashes are absent — [measurement:em-dashes] 0 instances, 0 per 1,000 words, 0/10 samples. Use the en-dash for mid-sentence breaks; do not use the em-dash.

## 7. What the corpus never does

Structure is carried entirely in prose — 10/10 samples. Each shift of subject or argument is marked by a new paragraph, usually opening on the new subject's name or a transitional phrase (`dickovers` moves from Reader Mode to Kill Sticky by opening a paragraph: *"That's Reader Mode…Now let's move on to more advanced techniques, starting with 'Kill Sticky.'"*). Nothing in the corpus breaks a piece with a heading or a bulleted list. If a section needs marking, start a new paragraph with the new subject.

The uncontracted negative form is near-absent — [measurement:uncontracted-negatives] 9 instances across the corpus, 0.51 per 1,000 words, against [measurement:contractions] 300 contracted forms, 17.09 per 1,000 words: a ratio of roughly 33:1. The near-absence is established across all 10 samples by the aggregate rate. A draft that reproduces the contraction rate while also producing uncontracted negatives at any ordinary English rate will not match this corpus. Write contracted; treat the uncontracted form as a marked choice.

Em-dashes are absent — [measurement:em-dashes] 0 instances, 0 per 1,000 words, 0/10 samples — against 73 en-dashes at 4.16 per 1,000 words. Both facts are needed: the en-dash rate is the target for mid-sentence interruption; the zero em-dash count means this substitution is not an option, not an oversight.

## 8. What this profile could not determine

The voice card was not filled in. All observations are derived from the corpus.

The corpus covers ten posts from a two-week window in July 2026. How the register behaves across a longer timeline, across subjects the writer is less certain about, or when addressing a hostile readership, is not visible here.

All ten samples are polemical blog posts. The profile does not describe how this voice behaves in book-length argument, fiction, or speeches, even though the author works in all three registers.

Three observations were dropped: a claimed preference for opening every paragraph with a noun phrase (present often but inconsistent enough that no reliable instruction follows); a claimed avoidance of the passive voice (the passive appears in all ten samples — *"are required to secure," "was informed," "being forced to"* — and is not a genuine absence); and a claimed pattern whereby the second paragraph always contradicts the first (it does this frequently but not consistently enough to count).
